name: Bagri
confidence_why: The only first-hand description of Bagri stress is Gusain's own fieldwork (1999 JNU thesis, condensed in the 2000 Lincom sketch), which places stress on the initial syllable of disyllabic nouns and the final syllable of disyllabic verbs with three minimal pairs, while cautioning that stress is a marginal feature in a language he treats as tonal; no other source addresses the question.
catalog_citation: Gusain, Lakhan. 1999. A Descriptive Grammar of Bagri. PhD thesis, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi. (archive.org item 20231025_20231025_1803: + djvu text layer)
catalog_locator: sec. 4.3.2 'Stress', thesis p. 196 (PDF page 204); summary restated in ch. 'Conclusion' ( line ~13659); tone in sec. 4.3.3 pp. 196-197
catalog_quote: 4.3.2 Stress. The stress is not an important feature of Bagri, yet, it seems that its existence and phonemic status cannot be ruled out. Stress is utilized in disyllabic syllables to distinguish between grammatical categories. In nouns, stress accent falls on the initial syllable and in the verb category stress accent falls on the final syllable. The stressed syllable is marked by the symbol [ˈ] Nouns: ˈbəlla 'evil spirit', ˈhilla 'job', ˈsilla 'rumour'; Verbs: bəˈlla 'call', hiˈlla 'cause to move', siˈlla 'cause to wet'. Phonetically, stress is employed to express emphasis. The phonetic correlate is the combination of length and pitch. Emphasized syllables contain a greater amount of energy. 4.3.3 Tones / Pitch. Bagri has developed tonal contrasts like Punjabi language. Though it is a very controversial aspect of the suprasegmentals of the Bagri, yet there are known to be three tones. …

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Bagri with an empty rule; this work supplies the first statement: marginal, category-conditioned stress (noun-initial, verb-final in disyllables) in a language the author treats as tonal. Note the open copy is the 1999 JNU thesis, not the 2000 Lincom print; the Lincom sketch is the published condensation of the same description by the same author, so the quote should be re-verified against the Lincom pages before it is attributed to the 2000 citation.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bagri is described as tonal (three tones, low/mid/high, 'like Punjabi', though the author calls this controversial). Word stress is called unimportant but possibly phonemic: in disyllables it distinguishes grammatical category, nouns stressed on the initial syllable, verbs on the final syllable (minimal pairs 'balla / ba'lla). Beyond that, stress is a sentence-level emphasis device (length + pitch); in a non-emphatic sentence all words get almost equal stress (p. 73) and the question word is always stressed (pp. 20, 102). Conclusion (Ch. 7): 'Tone is prominent in Bagri.. Stress is not an important feature in this language.'
new_statements.exceptions: Stress placement is stated only for disyllables and only as a noun-initial vs verb-final contrast; no rule for longer words. Emphatic/contrastive stress can fall on any constituent of a sentence (p. 73). Tone is said to be a 'very controversial aspect' of Bagri suprasegmentals.
new_statements.identity_note: Gusain 1999 describes Bagri as spoken across the Ganganagar/Hanumangarh belt of Rajasthan and adjoining Haryana and Punjab (maps 1-3), without singling out a sub-dialect. The archive.org open copy is his 1999 JNU PhD thesis 'A Descriptive Grammar of Bagri', the source text of the 2000 Lincom sketch listed in the catalog, not the Lincom print itself. Kumar 2020 is a Punjabi-language sociolinguistic study of Bagri in Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources: Kumar 2020 could not be read past its table of contents, and that TOC has no prosody section. Within Gusain 1999 there is an internal tension worth flagging: the same page says stress 'is not an important feature of Bagri' and that its 'phonemic status cannot be ruled out', then gives a category-based placement (noun-initial vs verb-final in disyllables) supported by three minimal pairs; the conclusion repeats 'Stress is not an important feature'. Gusain also calls Bagri tonal 'like Punjabi' while conceding tone is 'a very controversial aspect' of its suprasegmentals. The catalog itself has no rule for Bagri, so nothing there is contradicted.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim on the page image of thesis p. 196 (PDF p. 204) and in the djvu text layer; locator correct. The deciding source is the only full grammar of Bagri (Gusain 1999, JNU PhD, 253 pp, supervised by Abbi), which is also the source behind the published Lincom sketch; no dedicated stress/prosody or JIPA-type study of Bagri exists in Glottolog, Crossref, archive.org, Wikipedia's bibliography or Shodhganga. The classification 'morphological' (noun-initial vs verb-final stress in disyllables, stress otherwise marginal, tone prominent) faithfully reflects the source, including its hedge.
